newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Stricken Mir crew face two-week wait for help.
newsitem.headline: Stricken Mir crew face two-week wait for help.

text.p: The three men aboard Russia's stricken Mir space station on Thursday faced a bleak couple of weeks awaiting a relief ship to bring vital supplies needed for the repair of their damaged craft.

The crew prepared on Thursday for their second night since the Wednesday accident and were deciding on the best berth for U.S. astronaut Michael Foale, who had preferred to sleep in the Spektr scientific module until a Progress freighter pierced a hole in it, said Korolyov Mission Control Centre outside Moscow
The Spektr module is now sealed off from the rest of Mir.
A spokesman said Foale had not yet chosen a place to spend the night. "The most comfortable place is on the ceiling. It is usually given to a woman cosmonaut when there is one," he said.
Cramped conditions on Mir are far from ideal at the best of times. Foale has described it as "a very dirty and grimy camping trip in an old car".
The spokesman said the crew, also including mission commander Vasily Tsibliyev and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin, had been urged to get a good night's sleep after a stressful day.
The Mir team faces one of the most difficult crises in space since Apollo 13 came close to disaster in 1970.
The collision smashed one of four solar panels, cutting electricity by 25 to 30 percent in the whole station and forcing the crew to halt experiments and physical exercise.
Russian Space Agency chief Yuri Koptev said the cosmonauts were in no immediate danger and there were no plans to evacuate them after the worst accident in Mir's 11-year history.
But the crew will take to their Soyuz escape craft and return to Earth if the air pressure in their main accommodation falls below about three quarters of the current norm, he said.
Mission Control said they faced a "five-point emergency". A "seven" means abandon ship.

A Progress cargo craft will be launched in 11 days, carrying supplies to repair the damage, Koptev said. It will take it two days to reach Mir and even when the Progress arrives after a two-day journey the crew's problems may not be over.
A spokesman for Russia's Military Space Forces, which will launch the Progress, said Mir's low power would make the docking "very difficult".

A committee including NASA officials and Mir's designer met for three hours to fix details of the repair mission. Deputy mission chief Sergei Krikalyov told Reuters only Russian supplies, including specialised electric cables, were needed.

Krikalyov said after the meeting a detailed, concrete action plan was yet to be worked out, adding no welding operations had been planned. Some experts said the cosmonauts may make a space walk while waiting for the Progress.
It was due to start a routine trip on Friday but will now wait 10 more days for supplies at the Baikonur launch pad.
Marshal Yevgeny Shaposhnikov, who advises President Boris Yeltsin on space and aviation matters, visited the Mission Control and was expected to report to the Kremlin leader.
The Soviet-built Mir, which means both "Peace" and "World" in Russian, is caught in a vicious circle.

The collision knocked its solar panels out of line with the Sun, reducing its power. And with low power the crew were finding it hard to realign the ungainly 140-tonne complex of interconnecting modules.

Mission Control spokesman Valery Latyshev said all the experiments were cancelled to save power and the crew would no longer take the oxygen-burning exercise they normally have to do to combat the effects of weightlessness on the body.

If the crew were forced to evacuate it would recall memories of the 1970 Apollo 13 mission, when three U.S. astronauts abandoned ship after an explosion. As the world held its breath, they defied lengthy odds and made it home in a tiny lunar landing craft that was short on air, power and heating.
In Mir's case, however, the lifeboat is a state-of-the-art Soyuz TM-25, specifically designed for the return journey.
